Most people know except as a preposition — "Everyone passed except Tom." But used as a verb, it carries a slightly different quality: it describes an action — someone actively choosing to leave something out.

To except means to deliberately exclude or leave out a specific person or thing from a general statement, rule, group, or situation that otherwise applies to everything or everyone else.

Think of it this way: you're drawing a big circle that covers everything, and then you reach in and pull one thing out of it. That act of pulling it out — that's excepting it.
The Three Forms You'll Actually Encounter

1. "Excepted" (past participle — the most common form)

This is used when the excluded thing is mentioned directly before or after the word:

  • "Present company excepted, everyone at that party was rude."
    → Translation: "I'm not talking about the people with me right now — I'm leaving them out — but everyone else at that party was rude."
  • "All employees must work overtime, senior managers excepted."
    → Senior managers are being left out of this rule.
  • "The new policy applies to all departments, no one excepted."
    → Not a single person is being left out; it applies to absolutely everyone.

You'll notice excepted often sits at the end of a phrase or clause, doing quiet but important work — quietly saying "but not this one."

2. "Excepting" (present participle — used like "excluding")

This form works almost identically to the word excluding. It introduces the thing that's being left out:

  • "Excepting the first chapter, the book was wonderful."
    → Leave the first chapter aside; everything else was wonderful.
  • "All students, not excepting the top rankers, must sit the exam."
    → Even the top rankers — who might expect to be left out — are included. Nobody is excepted.

Notice that "not excepting X" means the opposite of what it might first seem: it means X is also included, not left out. "Not excepting the manager" means the manager is in too — no one is getting an exclusion.

3. Active verb: "to except" (direct action form)

This is less common in everyday speech but perfectly correct:

  • "The law excepts children under 12 from this requirement."
    → The law actively leaves children under 12 out of this rule.
  • "The company excepted senior staff from the new dress code."
    → Someone decided to leave senior staff out of the rule.

Here, a subject (the law, the company, a person) is the one doing the excepting.

You'll encounter "always excepting" as a set phrase that signals a standing, permanent exclusion — something that is always being left out whenever a general claim is made:

  • "The food at that restaurant is excellent — always excepting the desserts, which are too sweet."
    → Every time I praise that restaurant, I'm always leaving the desserts out of that praise.

It's a graceful way to say: "My general statement has one consistent exception."
The Second, Rarer Meaning: To Formally Object

In formal contexts — especially legal language — to except has a second meaning: to raise a formal objection; to officially say "I disagree with this" or "I protest this."

  • "The defense counsel excepted to the judge's ruling."
    → The defense lawyer formally objected to the judge's decision.
  • "She excepted to his version of events."
    → She formally protested the way he described what happened.

This comes from the same root idea: when you object to something, you are in effect removing yourself from agreement with it — excepting yourself from consent. In everyday modern speech, people would almost always say "objected to" instead. But if you ever read older literature, legal documents, or formal writing, you may encounter it — and now you'll recognize it.
How the Verb Differs from the Preposition

PrepositionVerb
Example"Everyone left except Tom.""The teacher excepted Tom from the test."
NatureStates a fact about exclusionDescribes the act of excluding
Who does the action?No one — it just isSomeone actively decides

The meaning is the same at heart — it's always about exclusion — but the verb form describes an intentional act by someone, rather than simply stating that something doesn't fit.

The verb to except means to actively leave something or someone out from a general rule, group, or statement. Its most common form is excepted (used in passive constructions like "present company excepted") and excepting (used like the word excluding). A rarer formal meaning is to raise a formal objection.

The heart of the word, in every use, is the same: something is being separated out from the general whole — and that separation is deliberate.
